set.t: The Virgin and Child Enthroned (Sant'Apollinare Nuovo)
set.l: Basilica of Sant'Apollinare Nuovo, Ravenna (in situ, lower register of the north wall)

summary: The Virgin sits frontally on a jewelled throne with a red cushion, wrapped in a dark purple mantle with small crosses on her brow, and holds the Christ Child upright on her lap. The Child, in a white and gold garment and a cross-nimbus, raises his right hand in blessing, while the hand of an attendant angel appears at the left edge. Set against a field of gold, the group is the goal of the long procession of virgins on the north wall of Theodoric's palace church, presenting Mary as the throne of the incarnate Lord.
facts: The basilica was built by the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great as his palace church and dedicated in 504 to Christ the Redeemer.

The procession of 22 virgins led by the three Magi that advances towards this group was made after the church had passed to orthodox (Catholic) use; the Magi there are named Balthasar, Melchior and Gaspar.
The nave mosaics were renovated, and in places altered, in the mid-19th century by Felice Kibel.

links.label: UNESCO: Early Christian Monuments of Ravenna

notes: The enthroned Virgin and Child and the facing Christ with angels are usually assigned to Theodoric's original decoration (c. 500–526), the processions to the later reworking under Bishop Agnellus; the 19th-century restoration means some details may be renewed. Commons gives an impossible photo date (2514).

set.t: Salus Populi Romani (Icon of the Virgin and Child)
set.d: original probably 6th–8th century (proposals range from the 5th to the 13th); overpainted c. 1100–13th century
set.l: Cappella Paolina (Borghese Chapel), Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore, Rome
set.m: Paint on cedar panel, heavily overpainted

summary: The half-length Virgin, in a dark blue, gold-edged mantle over a purple tunic, gazes directly at the viewer with her hands folded around the Christ Child, who sits on her left arm holding a closed book and raising his right hand in blessing. Greek letters at the top name her Mother of God. Rome's most venerated Marian icon, its present surface is largely medieval overpainting over a much older original, so that it carries centuries of devotion in its very layers.
facts: Scholars agree that the visible surface is largely medieval overpainting over an older original, which has been dated to almost every period between the 5th and 13th centuries; Gerhard Wolf cautiously calls the original 'probably Late Antique'.
At 117 × 79 cm on a thick cedar panel it is very large for an icon; by legend it is one of the 'Luke images' said to have been painted by St Luke.
It has been kept since 1613 in the Pauline Chapel built for it, and was cleaned and restored by the Vatican Museums, after which a Pontifical Mass was celebrated before it on 28 January 2018.
notes: Date strongly disputed. Wikidata records inceptions of 700 and 1000; the Wikipedia dating discussion points to a 7th-century original (with stylistic links to the 8th century) beneath overpainting of c. 1100–13th century. y=650 is a midpoint for the original layer. Wikidata's 'oil paint' medium is not supported and was replaced.

set.l: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (1991.366)

summary: A continuous frieze of closely packed figures in tunics and togas runs along the front of this marble sarcophagus. Near the centre Christ rides a donkey into Jerusalem, with a figure in a tree above and a youth spreading a garment before him; to the right, baskets of loaves stand at the feet of the apostles, and at the far right Lazarus, wrapped like a mummy, stands in the doorway of a temple-fronted tomb. At the left, soldiers in flat caps lead a bearded man away, a scene usually read as the arrest of Peter. Such sarcophagi show how quickly, in the decades after Constantine, Roman sculptors turned the Gospel into a language of salvation for the dead.
facts: The Met dates the sarcophagus to the early 300s and notes that it has undergone modern restoration.
It measures 67.3 × 212.1 × 61.9 cm and was given to the Museum by Josef and Marsy Mittlemann in 1991.

links.label: The Met: Sarcophagus with Scenes from the Lives of Saint Peter and Christ

notes: Scene identifications (Entry into Jerusalem, Multiplication of the Loaves, Raising of Lazarus, Arrest of Peter, and at the far left probably Peter's miracle of the spring with a kneeling soldier drinking) are read from the visible iconography; the Met's online label text was not available. Some heads and details are modern restorations.

set.t: The Virgin and Child between the Archangels Michael and Gabriel (Apse Mosaic, Panagia Angeloktisti, Kiti)
set.l: Church of Panagia Angeloktisti, Kiti, Cyprus (in situ, apse)

summary: In the half-dome of the apse the Virgin stands on a footstool against a gold ground, holding the Christ Child on her left arm, between two archangels in white robes who bear sceptres and offer orbs. The inscription above her reads HAGIA MARIA, and a decorative border runs along the base of the conch. Surviving from an early Christian basilica and built into the later church, it is one of the finest early Byzantine wall mosaics in Cyprus and a rare survivor of the age before Iconoclasm.
facts: The apse of a 5th-century basilica, with its 6th-century mosaic, was incorporated into the later Byzantine church (11th century), which is why the mosaic survived the basilica's destruction.
The Virgin is labelled HAGIA MARIA ('Holy Mary') rather than Theotokos; the archangels' wings are rendered like peacock feathers, and the border shows a Fountain of Life with ducks, parrots and deer.
The church was placed on Cyprus's tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage in 2015.
notes: Dated on stylistic grounds (Megaw) to the 6th century, probably its later part; some writers date it to the 7th. The photograph shows the whole apse at a distance.

set.t: Bust of Christ between Alpha and Omega (Catacomb of Commodilla)
set.l: Catacomb of Commodilla, Via delle Sette Chiese, Rome (in situ)

summary: Framed in a square panel on a ceiling, Christ appears as a bust with long hair parted in the middle, a full dark beard and a large pale nimbus, gazing calmly out at the viewer. The Greek letters alpha and omega stand to either side of his head. Painted in a Roman burial chamber, it is one of the early images of Christ in the mature, bearded type that later became standard, and it proclaims him as the beginning and end of all things to those laid to rest beneath it.
facts: The alpha and omega beside the head quote Christ's words in Revelation: 'I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end'.

The Commodilla catacomb was used as a cemetery in the second half of the 4th century, became a pilgrimage site for the martyrs Felix and Adauctus, and was abandoned after their relics were removed under Pope Leo IV (847–855).
Rediscovered by Antonio Bosio in 1595, the catacomb yielded a further painted area, including the richly frescoed cubiculum of Leo, in 1953.
notes: Dated 'late 4th century' by the Commons description; the exact chamber is not named there (it is often linked with the cubiculum of Leo, which could not be confirmed from the sources read). Image sourced from a secondary website, so check rights if a better photo is found.
